"You can’t talk about the Pacific Crest Trail without mentioning the crowds," Pete Brook writes for Outside. But after the movie, starring Reese Witherspoon, was released in 2014, interest in the PCT exploded. "Millions are hearing about it now and are being inspired," Haskel said. Strayed, more or less unprepared for the journey, hiked 1,100 miles of the trail as a form of therapy as she grappled with personal demons. details.ground_truth: Scientists are now saying there may have been "a more colorful Jurassic World than we previously imagined," thanks to the recent discovery of a fossil in China's Hebei province. Reuters reports that a closer look at the "exquisitely preserved," almost completely intact fossil of a crow-like dinosaur that lived about 161 million years ago revealed that Caihong juji had luminous, brilliantly hued feathers that closely resembled those of hummingbirds. The study in the journal Nature Communications documenting the find explains that "Caihong" means "rainbow" in Mandarin. Scientists think the colorful plumage, which appeared to have covered the bony-crested creature's head, neck, and chest areas, may have kept the dinosaur warm, as well as attracted potential mates; National Geographic compares it to peacock feathers. So how were researchers able to tell what color feathers the creature had from preserved bones? They used high-tech microscopes able to home in on 66 sites on the fossil, detecting tiny cell structures called melanosomes, which underlie pigmentation. Which colors they led to can be found by their shapes, and the melanosomes in Caihong were long and flat like pancakes—similar to those found in hummingbirds, which boast iridescent plumage. Although they can't pick out from the Pantone wheel Caihong's exact colors, researchers say the creature likely sported feathers with a "rainbow glimmer." Study co-author Xing Zu tells National Geographic that Caihong was a predator that spent its days gliding from tree to tree. And "glide" is the operative word, as this dinosaur likely didn't fly: Its feathers were located on its tail, not on its wings like birds, Discover notes. (A study postulated that nearly all dinosaurs had feathers.)

**New Study Suggests Acetaminophen May Increase Risk of ADHD in Children**

A recent study published in the American Medical Association journal JAMA Pediatrics has found that frequent use of acetaminophen, a common pain reliever, during pregnancy may be associated with an increased risk of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in children. The study, which analyzed data from over 64,000 children, found that mothers who used acetaminophen for more than 20 times a week had a 29% higher risk of their child being diagnosed with ADHD. The study also found that mothers who used acetaminophen for more than 20 weeks during pregnancy had a 50% increased risk of their child developing ADHD.

**Researchers Warn Against Overuse, Not Abstinence**

While the study's findings are concerning, researchers emphasize that the results do not suggest a cause-and-effect relationship between acetaminophen use and ADHD. Instead, they recommend that pregnant women use the medication judiciously and avoid overuse. "We aren't saying that pregnant women should never take acetaminophen," said Dr. Beate Ritz, the study's author. "But if you're taking it frequently, you might want to consider alternatives."

**Experts Suggest Alternatives to Acetaminophen**

Experts recommend that pregnant women consider non-pharmacological ways to manage pain, such as massages, baths, and acupuncture. "There are non-pharmacological ways to deal with pain," said Dr. Jeffrey Chapa, head of maternal-fetal medicine at Cleveland Clinic Children's Hospital. "I think we have to focus a little bit more on that as opposed to just medications."

**Manufacturer Responds to Study**

The manufacturer of Tylenol, McNeil Consumer Healthcare, has responded to the study, stating that there is no prospective, randomized controlled study that has found a causal link between acetaminophen use during pregnancy and ADHD in children. The company emphasizes that Tylenol has a favorable safety profile when used as directed.

**More Research Needed**

While the study's findings are intriguing, researchers acknowledge that more research is needed to fully understand the relationship between acetaminophen use and ADHD in children. "We need more studies to understand the potential risks and benefits of acetaminophen use during pregnancy," said Dr. Ritz.

details.ground_truth: NASA is going to the sun. More specifically, it's launching an unmanned probe next year that will travel closer to the star than any spacecraft has done previously. "It's a spacecraft loaded with technological breakthroughs that will solve many of the largest mysteries about our star," says Nicola Fox of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. In less scientific terms, per the Telegraph: "We will finally touch the sun." The nuts and bolts: The mission: The 10-foot probe will launch in July or August of 2018 and eventually get to within 3.7 million miles of the sun, about seven times closer than any previous spacecraft. Eventually, it will be whizzing around the sun at a speed of 450,000 miles per hour, reports CNN. The mission ends in 2025. Corona: The probe will actually fly into the outermost part of the sun's atmosphere, called the corona, per a mission overview at NASA that touts "humanity's first visit to a star." The heat: The probe will rely on a 4.5-inch-thick carbon-composite solar shield to help it withstand temperatures up to 2,550 degrees Fahrenheit, reports Orlando's WKMG. Instruments will remain at room temperature. The name: The probe's name has been changed to the Parker Solar Probe to honor astrophysicist Eugene Parker, who's credited with discovering solar wind. Parker, who turns 90 in June, is a professor emeritus at the University of Chicago, and the Guardian recounts that the theory he put forward in 1958 about a stream of charged particles flowing from the sun was once thought to be "crazy." A first: This is the first time NASA has named a mission after a living scientist. "I'm certainly greatly honored," said the man himself, per Space.com. Two puzzles: Scientists hope to better understand two things in particular: "How is the solar wind accelerated, and why is the ... corona so much hotter than the solar surface?" (It's 3 million degrees Fahrenheit vs. 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit.) Why it matters: Generally, solar storms are relatively harmless when they reach Earth, but these particle bursts occasionally wreak havoc on satellites and here on Earth, and they have the potential to be devastating. "The more we know about how these processes work, the better we can get at predicting when they will happen," writes Loren Grush at the Verge.

According to historical sources, John the Apostle was a favorite among Early Christians, and his grave in Ephesus was a major pilgrimage site.

The Burgas fortress and port was first excavated in 2008 by Bulgarian archaeologists. The site has a complex history, with the fortress being used as a military base and later as a monastery. While the dwarf planet tries to fight its way back into the good graces of Those Who Deem What Counts as a Planet, another icy orb even further out may snatch that designation first. Astronomers at the California Institute of Technology say a giant celestial body "lurking at the end of our solar system," as the Washington Post puts it, may actually be a planet, and they're even already calling it "Planet Nine." The charred remains of the victims were found in a warehouse, with many of the bodies unrecognizable.

**Yo-Yo Dieting Linked to Increased Risk of Heart Attacks, Strokes, and Death in People with Coronary Artery Disease**

A recent study published in The New England Journal of Medicine has found that rapidly losing and gaining weight, also known as yo-yo dieting, can significantly increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and death in people with coronary artery disease (CAD). The study, which followed 9,509 men and women with CAD over a period of five years, found that those who experienced the largest fluctuations in weight had a 78% higher risk of developing new-onset diabetes, a 124% higher risk of death, and a 78% higher risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Coronary artery disease is a condition in which the arteries that supply blood to the heart become narrowed or blocked, leading to heart attacks and strokes. The study's findings suggest that maintaining a stable weight is crucial for people with CAD, and that repeated weight loss and gain can have serious health consequences.

The researchers, led by Dr. Sripal Bangalore, found that the risk of adverse outcomes increased with the magnitude of weight fluctuations. Those who experienced the largest weight fluctuations had a 124% higher risk of death, compared to those who experienced the smallest weight fluctuations.

The study's findings are consistent with previous research that has linked yo-yo dieting to poor heart health. However, this study is the first to specifically examine the relationship between weight fluctuations and outcomes in people with CAD.

The researchers note that their study is observational, and that more research is needed to determine the underlying causes of the association between yo-yo dieting and poor health outcomes. However, they suggest that the findings warrant further investigation and highlight the importance of maintaining a stable weight for people with CAD.

**Key Findings:**

* Yo-yo dieting increases the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and death in people with coronary artery disease.
* The risk of adverse outcomes increases with the magnitude of weight fluctuations.
* Those who experienced the largest weight fluctuations had a 124% higher risk of death.
* Maintaining a stable weight is crucial for people with CAD.

**Recommendations:**

* People with CAD should aim to maintain a stable weight through a healthy diet and regular exercise.
* Healthcare providers should counsel patients with CAD on the importance of weight management and provide support to help them achieve and maintain a healthy weight.
* Further research is needed to determine the underlying causes of the association between yo-yo dieting and poor health outcomes.
details.ground_truth: Losing weight is one thing, keeping it off quite another. And now researchers are finding that among those with coronary heart disease (CHD)—which the Mayo Clinic reports develops from damaged or diseased blood vessels typically caused by blockage and inflammation—yo-yo dieting may dramatically increase the risk of stroke, heart attack, and death. Reporting in the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers say they followed nearly 10,000 men and women with CHD between the ages of 35 and 75 for about five years, monitoring changes in body weight and other health outcomes. The takeaway? "It's important to lose weight, but this data says you have to keep it off," lead researcher Dr. Sripal Bangalore at the New York University School of Medicine tells the New York Times. The highest weight fluctuation was on average 8.6 pounds over five years, while the smallest body weight changes averaged closer to two pounds, reports Medical News Today. Those who were already overweight or obese at the beginning of the study and who experienced the highest level of weight fluctuation experienced 124% more deaths, 136% more strokes, and 117% more heart attacks, meaning these CHD patients were more than twice as likely to suffer these negative outcomes in just a few years than people with CHD whose weight only fluctuated two pounds. This doesn't pinpoint a cause, as pre-existing heart problems could be the culprit, but researchers hope to study this correlation further. (Yo-yo dieting is bad for women's hearts in general.)

A devastating incident at a Hawaii dentist's office has left a family grieving and seeking answers. Additionally, the family claims that no one administered CPR to Finley after she went into cardiac arrest.

The medical examiner's office has ruled the death an accident, but the family is seeking justice and accountability. Dr. Geyer's attorney has called the allegations "unproven" but has declined to comment further due to the lawsuit.

The incident has sparked a review of dental sedation practices in Hawaii, with new state rules taking effect in January 2014 to tighten oversight of dental sedation. The family's tragedy serves as a reminder of the importance of proper medical care and monitoring, especially when it comes to vulnerable patients like children.

No criminal charges have been brought against Dr. Geyer, but the family's lawsuit seeks to hold her accountable for the tragic events that unfolded at the dentist's office.

The aftermath of Katrina was devastating, with widespread destruction and loss of life. Ricks, a lifelong resident of New Orleans, was heartbroken by the response to the disaster, which he felt was inadequate. He and his colleagues worked tirelessly to help those affected, but the experience left a lasting impact on the community.

Today, Ricks is back at work, reflecting on the lessons learned from Katrina. The storm was a wake-up call for the National Weather Service, and it has since made significant improvements in its emergency forecasting and communication. A recent study has found that colon cancer rates are increasing among men and women under the age of 50, a trend that is challenging the traditional perception of colon cancer as a disease that primarily affects older adults. According to the study, one in seven colon cancer patients in the US is now under the age of 50, and this number is expected to rise to one in four by 2030.

Researchers analyzed data from over 258,000 patients diagnosed with colon cancer between 1998 and 2011 and found that younger patients were more likely to be diagnosed with advanced stage cancer, but they also tended to live slightly longer than older patients. The study's lead author, Dr. Samantha Hendren, notes that this may be due to the fact that younger patients are more likely to receive aggressive treatment.

The study's findings have significant implications for colon cancer screening guidelines, which currently recommend that adults begin screening at age 50. However, some experts are questioning whether this age threshold is still appropriate, given the rising rates of colon cancer among younger adults.

Dr. Hendren suggests that doctors should be on the lookout for warning signs of colon cancer, such as rectal bleeding, and that people with a family history of colon cancer should begin screening earlier than age 50. However, other experts, such as Dr. Andrew Chan, caution that the data is not yet strong enough to support expanding screening to younger age groups.

The study's findings also highlight the need for increased awareness and education about colon cancer among younger adults, as well as the importance of early detection and treatment. As Dr. Hendren notes, "the cancer community needs to prepare for the increasing number of very young colorectal cancer survivors who will need long-term support to cope with the physical and psychological consequences of their disease and treatments."

**Ancient Human Behaviors and Technological Advancements in Africa**

Recent discoveries in Kenya's Olorgesailie Basin have shed new light on the evolution of human behavior and technological advancements in Africa. The findings, published in three papers in the journal Science, suggest that early humans in the region were more advanced and sophisticated than previously thought.

**Middle Stone Age Tools**

The oldest tools found in the region date back to around 320,000 years ago, challenging the long-held view that the Middle Stone Age began tens of thousands of years later. The tools, which include hand axes, points, and blades, demonstrate a level of technological sophistication and planning, indicating a high degree of social complexity. The researchers believe that these tools were made possible by the exchange of ideas and materials over long distances, facilitated by the presence of complex social networks.

**Climate Change and Technological Advancements**

The team suggests that the technological advancements in the region were a response to climate change. The Olorgesailie Basin was a region of great geological upheaval, with frequent earthquakes and droughts. The researchers propose that the early humans adapted to these environmental pressures by developing new tools and behaviors, which were then passed on to other groups.

**Implications**

The findings have significant implications for our understanding of human evolution. They suggest that the "human revolution" may have occurred much earlier than previously thought, with complex behaviors and technological advancements emerging in Africa, not just in Europe. The research also highlights the importance of considering the African archaeological record in the context of human evolution.

**Key Findings**

* The Middle Stone Age tools in the Olorgesailie Basin date back to around 320,000 years ago.
* The tools demonstrate a high level of technological sophistication and planning.
* The presence of complex social networks and long-distance exchange of ideas and materials is suggested.
* The findings challenge the long-held view that the Middle Stone Age began tens of thousands of years later.

details.ground_truth: For decades, the human story was one told through signs of modernity—art, tools, burials—found only after Homo sapiens left Africa. Recent discoveries pushing back the date of departure are helping to change that narrative, as are three new studies in Science. Together, they describe the earliest stone tools of their kind in East Africa as well as the earliest evidence for long-distance transport of raw materials in the region, per Science News. Researchers previously believed the Early Stone Age marked by large, primitive tools (hand axes and cleavers) made way for the Middle Stone Age and its smaller tools (spearpoints and blades) around 280,000 years ago. But stone tools found in Kenya's Olorgesailie Basin show hominin groups—it's not clear which species is responsible—had developed these more advanced tools approximately 320,000 years ago. "We see a smaller technology, a more diverse series of stone tools … designed for specific purposes," researcher Rick Potts tells NPR. An expert not involved in the study says the tools are so "prepared and retouched" they suggest the Middle Stone Age likely started even earlier. What drove it? Microscopic and chemical analyses of the region's soil show the landscape was rapidly shifting between wet and dry conditions, meaning hominins might have been forced to adapt. But as the technology also coincides with the emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa, it's possible that the human mind deserves credit. The tools themselves suggest the development of trading networks, too. Some were made of rocks carried from 55 miles away, says Potts. Others were made of obsidian from as far as 30 miles away, per the Conversation. (These stone tools are also making waves.)

Jumaah, who had been working on his PhD at Lund University, was able to complete his studies and now works for a pharmaceuticals company in Malmö. His family has almost finished paying back the university for the rescue operation.

Turner's actions were motivated by her concern for her student's safety and her outrage at the actions of ISIS. "What was happening was completely unacceptable," she said. details.ground_truth: The final round of voting began in Egypt today, and it looks like the Muslim Brotherhood could walk off with a controlling majority of seats in Parliament's lower house. The Muslim Brotherhood's Freedom and Justice Party, the country's mainstream Islamist party, had already won a high percentage of the seats awarded in the first and second rounds of voting. Two of the nine provinces voting today are Brotherhood strongholds, where some of the party's most well-known candidates are running, the New York Times reports. A plurality, not a majority, was originally predicted for the Freedom and Justice Party. A majority would allow the party to govern alone, but the Brotherhood has repeatedly said it plans to form a coalition government, and has aligned itself with more liberal parties rather than the ultraconservative Salafis, who are in second place with up to 25% of the seats so far. Also today, prosecutors began presenting their case against former Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, Bloomberg notes. His trial resumed last week after a two-month break; state TV today showed Mubarak being carried to and from the courtroom on a gurney. "He deserves an end of humiliation and indignity," said the chief prosecutor, according to the AP.

**LOCAL NEWS SUMMARY**

**CAR SUSPENDED FROM TELEPHONE POLE IN MENDON**

A bizarre incident occurred in Mendon on Wednesday evening when a car was suspended from a telephone guy wire after the driver reacted too quickly to a GPS unit's instructions. Nabila Altahan, the driver of a Toyota Corolla, was heading westbound on Route 4 when her GPS device suddenly directed her to turn around, as she had passed her intended destination. Altahan's quick reaction to the directions caused her to leave the road, and the car ended up suspended from the guy wire of a telephone pole across from Sugar & Spice Restaurant.

Fortunately, neither Altahan nor her passenger was injured in the incident. State Police and the Rutland City Fire Department responded to the scene, and a witness at the nearby miniature golf course reported seeing the driver jump out of the car as it was suspended from the pole.

This unusual incident serves as a reminder to drivers to exercise caution when following GPS directions, and to take a moment to consider the consequences of sudden actions on the road.

**NO OTHER NEWS REPORTED**
